sentences.text: Dealers monitor the largest absolute position reached before a review horizon ends.
We compare conditional quantile models with historical rules using hourly FX positions, weekly New York Fed positions and dealer aggregates in 17 CFTC futures markets.
Histories and update schedules are matched.
Historical rules are hard to beat.
First, FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8% and 16.6% across two periods, but its ranking against a shorter rolling rule changes.
Second, historical rules beat regression in 34 of 48 New York Fed comparisons and 29 of 34 CFTC comparisons; finite-penalty hindsight still favors history in most short weekly comparisons.
They usually remain in the model confidence set alongside alternatives.
In calibrated simulations, expanding the penalty menu cuts the constant-parameter median excess loss from 116.2% to near zero; switching adds no observed median loss in this short-history comparison.
Third, in CFTC, lower scores need not mean lower limit costs: higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor expanded regression.
The evidence is retrospective, and the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.

The evidence is retrospective, and the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.
Position limits must cover exposure between reviews.
A position that finishes inside a limit can still breach it earlier, so an endpoint forecast answers a different question from a forecast of the intervening peak.
We study the largest sampled absolute net position and compare all procedures on that same response.
A selected Treasury-bill path that returns within the reported historical limit at its endpoint after an intervening breach.
The rule chooses the earliest eligible original evaluation window.
Endpoint containment can conceal a peak breach.
Conditional models can use recent position states and calendar information to adapt a limit.
Estimating those relationships also uses a finite history, while a historical rule can be competitive without estimating many slopes.
The practical question is when the extra conditioning improves on an explicit historical benchmark, rather than whether a complex model fits the past well.
We examine one market maker's FX record and two official dealer reporting systems.
New York Fed reports describe government-securities positions, while CFTC categories describe aggregate dealer positions in futures markets.
Their economic units and information dates differ, so comparisons keep their own targets, scales and historical references.
Neither weekly system provides a collection of independent individual dealers.

The central finding is conditional: history, the tested penalty menu and stated limit costs organize the comparisons, but they do not establish a universally sufficient history or a uniquely causal explanation.
Matched FX gains coexist with adverse weekly comparisons and with reversals at the longest tested histories.
Historical rules remain a demanding benchmark across these records.
The first contribution is to connect the history-length evidence with an additional reporting system.
Earlier simulations support the registered short-history and long-history loss-sign predictions, while their universal simplification claim fails.
FX learning curves give a similarly qualified pattern.
The new CFTC extension agrees with the short-history counts but misses the registered long-history win target and the strict-improvement target.
The combined CFTC verdict is partial agreement, not validation of a universal history threshold.
The second contribution is to distinguish history from the available procedures.
An expanded penalty menu removes much of a short-history simulation loss, while financial diagnostics retain both selection errors and losses within the finite menu.
Access to an ordinary historical quantile is part of that expanded menu, so near-parity performance alone does not establish the value of extra predictors.
Related forecast comparisons leave historical methods alongside many uneliminated alternatives.
The third contribution is to connect forecast comparisons to stated limit costs.
Reserve amounts, breach frequency and exceedance magnitude enter separately.
Their weights can change which tested report is cheaper, and local exceptions remain.
These are hypothetical preferences rather than measured funding gains or an evaluated trading intervention.
Matching training-label histories and refit schedules makes the benchmark explicit.
It does not equalize every feature's raw history or every validation calculation, and it does not isolate a causal feature effect.
